question: A team stores an internal admin URL and the rule "only managers may see salaries" in the system prompt, trusting the model to keep both private. Which OWASP entry describes the risk, and what is the fix?
options: Misinformation; ask the model to double-check
Hidden Context Exposure (System Prompt Leakage in the 2025 edition): assume hidden context can be extracted; keep secrets out of it and enforce access rules in code
Unbounded Consumption; shorten the prompt
Vector and Embedding Weaknesses; re-embed the prompt
explanation: Instructions the user cannot see are still extractable through injection or clever questions. Authorization that only lives in a prompt is not authorization.

question: An email agent reads a message that tells it to forward the user's invoices to an outside address, and it does. Which entries apply most directly?
options: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses only
ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack (its objective was redirected by content it read) and Prompt Injection, with ASI02 Tool Misuse for the forwarding
Unbounded Consumption
ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication
explanation: Indirect injection is the cause, goal hijack is what it does to an agent, and the email tool is the instrument. Tagging all three helps link the incident to the controls that should have stopped it.

question: What does the Agentic Top 10 cover that the LLM list mostly does not?
options: Nothing: it renames the LLM list

Risks that appear when models plan and act: tool chains, delegated identities, runtime supply chains, memory that persists across runs, agent-to-agent messages, cascading failures, manipulation of human approvers and rogue agents
Only model training risks
Only regulatory compliance
explanation: The agentic list extends the LLM list to autonomy, tools, memory and multi-agent systems. A chat feature needs the first list; an agent needs both.

question: A support agent asks the on-call engineer to approve 40 refunds an hour, each with a confident, well-written justification. After a week the engineer approves without reading. Which agentic risk is this?
options: ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation: the human check erodes through fatigue and persuasive output, so it no longer protects anything
ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution
ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication
Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
explanation: Approvals are a control only while people read them. Fewer, higher-signal approvals, limits that do not need a human, and audits of approval rates keep the check real.

question: Two scanners report the same risk, one as LLM05 and the other as LLM10. What explains it, and what should the team record?
options: One scanner is wrong; discard its findings
The scanners cite different editions of the list, because ids and order change between editions; record the edition next to every id
LLM05 and LLM10 are two separate risks that happen to look alike
The model changed its own classification between runs
explanation: The lists are shared vocabulary, and their ids and order change between editions, so an id means something only together with its edition. Map the risk area by name and write the edition beside the id so findings compare across tools and teams.

question: How should a threat model use the two lists?
options: Copy the twenty entries as the threat model
Walk every entry and record whether it is not applicable, mitigated (by which control) or accepted (and why), and tag threats with the ids so findings compare across teams
Use only the first three entries of each list
Ignore them for internal tools
explanation: The value of a checklist is finding the entry you had not thought about, and leaving a trace of why each one does or does not apply.
